claims.text: Cooling phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys at rates exceeding 10^6 K/s will improve their glass-forming ability.
Cooling at rates exceeding 10^6 K/s will enhance the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state.
Conventional casting of the target alloys yields partially crystalline or metastable microstructures.
Rapid quenching by melt spinning can produce an amorphous state in the target alloys.
The intervention should be conducted under an inert atmosphere.
The intervention is expected to work when the alloy composition is near its critical-cooling-rate window.
Rapid quenching produces a highly disordered amorphous structure.
The rapidly quenched structure has minimized long-range atomic diffusion.
The rapidly quenched structure has a reduced density of heterogeneous nucleation sites.
Rapid quenching locks in a metastable atomic configuration by reducing the time available for diffusion.
Reduced diffusion time suppresses the nucleation and growth of crystalline phases.
Rapid quenching increases the free-energy barrier for atomic rearrangement.
The increased barrier for atomic rearrangement raises the crystallization onset temperature.
Rapidly quenched samples will have a higher DSC crystallization onset temperature than conventionally cast samples.
Rapidly quenched samples will exhibit less crystalline content than conventionally cast samples.
The intervention will lower the alloy's critical cooling rate.
The benefit is restricted to an optimal range of phosphorus and accompanying-element concentrations.
An insufficient cooling rate may fail to prevent crystallization.
